items.title: Macron calls for 'calm and order' after riots across France
items.tldr: French President Emmanuel Macron urged calm after a weekend of protests that escalated into rioting, looting, and arson, leaving at least 2,400 arrests, extensive property damage, and deepening political divisions ahead of the April 2027 elections.
items.background: The unrest erupted on Saturday when roughly 550,000 demonstrators gathered for largely peaceful protests against soaring fuel prices, a rising cost of living, and deteriorating public services. The movement, initially driven by student grievances, quickly merged with trade‑union and anti‑government factions. The resulting violence—car fires, building arson, and widespread looting—marked one of the most severe episodes of civil disorder in modern French history. The crisis arrives at a critical political juncture, with France preparing for a tightly contested April 2027 election that pits the hard‑right National Rally against the hard‑left La France Insoumise, amplifying existing ideological fissures.

analysis.heading: Political Context and Electoral Dynamics
analysis.content: The protests and subsequent riots have intensified the polarized electoral landscape. President Macron’s call for “calm and order” attempts to position the incumbent as a stabilizing force amid a backdrop of escalating discontent. Opposition leaders such as Marine Le Pen (National Rally) and Jean‑Luc Mélenchon (La France Insoumise) have seized the moment to critique government handling, framing the violence as a symptom of broader policy failures. This dynamic is likely to reshape campaign narratives, with each side emphasizing law‑and‑order versus socio‑economic justice themes, potentially influencing voter turnout and coalition‑building in the lead‑up to the April 2027 ballot.

analysis.heading: Socio‑Economic Drivers of Unrest
analysis.content: At its core, the unrest reflects deep‑seated economic pressures. Fuel price hikes, accelerated by global oil market volatility, have rippled through household budgets, compounding existing cost‑of‑living strains. The protest’s expansion from student‑led actions to include trade‑union and broader anti‑government groups underscores a convergence of grievances: education funding cuts, deteriorating public services, and perceived governmental indifference. The scale of the violence—arson of historic landmarks like the 19th‑century Limoges city hall—demonstrates how economic distress can morph into cultural‑heritage vandalism, signaling a loss of social cohesion that transcends mere policy disagreement.

analysis.heading: Technology and Governance: AI, Surveillance, and Regulation Implications
analysis.content: The French government’s response will likely accelerate debates on the role of AI‑driven crowd‑monitoring and predictive policing technologies. While interior minister Laurent Nuñez has highlighted the “outrages” committed by “several thousand far‑left individuals,” critics warn that deploying AI analytics without robust oversight could erode civil liberties. The incident also underscores the urgency of regulatory frameworks governing AI‑enabled risk analytics, especially as private firms such as OpenAI, Gemini, and Anthropic are increasingly involved in public‑safety contracts. Policymakers must balance security imperatives with transparency, potentially invoking the EU’s AI Act to set standards for deployment, data handling, and accountability in crisis scenarios.

key_facts: Approximately 550,000 demonstrators participated in largely peaceful protests before the violence escalated.
Police have arrested around 2,400 individuals; about 1,000 officers were injured, seven seriously.
Historic buildings, including Limoges city hall, were set ablaze, causing extensive heritage damage.
The unrest spans major cities: Paris, Marseille, Lille, and Lyon, with looting and clashes persisting into Sunday.
Political figures, including Marine Le Pen and Jean‑Luc Mélenchon, have used the crisis to critique governmental competence.
implications: Heightened political polarization could reshape the platform of both hard‑right and hard‑left parties in the upcoming 2027 election.
Potential legislative push for AI‑assisted surveillance and crowd‑control technologies may intensify, prompting new regulatory debates.
Economic policy adjustments—particularly around fuel pricing and social spending—will be under scrutiny as a means to restore public confidence.
items.outlook: In the short term, France faces a delicate balance between restoring public order and addressing underlying socio‑economic grievances. Internationally, the episode serves as a case study for how democratic societies manage mass unrest amid rapid technological advancement. Over the medium term, the interplay of electoral politics, AI governance, and economic policy will determine whether France can stabilize or drift toward deeper fragmentation.

Macron calls for 'calm and order' after riots across France
- Published
French President Emmanuel Macron has called for "calm and order" after a major day of protests turned into rioting and looting on Saturday, and as some disorder continued in Paris on Sunday.
In a national address from the ÃlysÃ©e Palace, he warned those who had taken part not to "escalate", adding: "We all feel anger and shame."
Some 550,000 demonstrators took to the streets for largely peaceful protests against rising fuel prices, the cost of living and deteriorating public services, including schools.
Macron said a distinction must be drawn between the "legitimate demands" of protesters and "those who destroyed, smashed and looted".
Police have arrested about 2,400 people, according to France's interior ministry.
The French president said "nothing justifies" the "unbridled" violence seen and said those involved would face justice.
Groups of rioters, some dressed in black and wearing masks and balaclavas, also came out in Paris, Marseille and other towns and cities, with some setting fire to cars and buildings.
On Sunday, looting and clashes with police continued on a smaller scale in parts of the capital and Lyon.
Tear gas and stun grenades were fired at hundreds of people in Paris, according to the AFP news agency, and bottles and rocks were again hurled at police.
Sunday saw cities across the country confront the impact of what developed into one of the worst bouts of disorder in modern French history.
In Limoges, the ornate 19th Century city hall was gutted by a fire started by rioters on Saturday, its clock tower and roof collapsing and the flames took hold.
Speaking near the ruined building, AnnÃ¨yse said: "This is very upsetting. Harming heritage buildings just because you are angry at the government is selfish, I think. It's hurting everybody."
"It's awful and unbelievable," said another man who gave his name as Gerrard. "We are very sad and I think it will be a long time to put it back as it was before."
Shopkeepers were seen early on Sunday morning picking up large shards of glass in Paris as rubbish trucks cleared up debris on some of the larger streets.
Widespread looting took place across the cities of Paris, Marseille and Lille, as well as other areas.
Macron said local prefects and mayors would draft measures to protect shops and civic buildings.
The president also said there would be "full transparency" over the police response to the demonstrations.
Tear gas and water cannon were turned on crowds over the weekend and riot police were seen hitting people with batons in several places.
France's interior ministry said about 1,000 police officers were injured on Saturday, seven of them seriously.
Student protests which began last month escalated significant on Saturday after they were joined by trade union members and other anti-government groups.
The response from political figures has pointed to France's deep political divisions as the country prepares for an election in April which could see the hard-right pitted against the hard-left.
France's Interior Minister Laurent NuÃ±ez said that while demonstrating was a fundamental right, there were "outrages" committed by "several thousand far-left individuals" who were determined to target public buildings and confront the police.
Later, they were joined by "delinquents who looted and ransacked numerous businesses in several cities in France", he said.
Jean-Luc MÃ©lenchon - leader of the hard-left La France Insoumise party - heavily criticised NuÃ±ez and police chiefs on social media.
He said they had "shown complete incompetence" with their handling of the demonstrations and called them "specialists in organised chaos".
Meanwhile, the leader of the hard-right National Rally party, Marine Le Pen, condemned the "exploitation" of anger "by political forces that encourage violence".

items.title: 'Very upsetting': Residents in shock after historic French town hall set alight
items.tldr: A 19th‑century town hall in Limoges was deliberately burned during a wave of nationwide protests, leaving the spire collapsed and the building’s fate uncertain. Residents describe the act as a selfish assault on heritage, while authorities investigate potential links to broader social unrest.
items.background: The incident unfolded on Saturday amid a series of protests that have swept France in response to recent policy reforms, particularly in the areas of public sector pensions and housing affordability. Limoges, a city renowned for its historic architecture and pharmaceutical industry, has long prided itself on the preservation of its municipal landmarks. The town hall, built in the 1800s, is not only an administrative centre but also a symbol of civic identity and cultural continuity for the community.

analysis.heading: Immediate Security Response
analysis.content: In the hours following the blaze, French fire services and local police deployed rapid response teams to contain the damage and secure the surrounding area. Footage posted online showed the building engulfed in flames, with the clock‑tower spire collapsing under the intensity of the fire. Firefighters, who battled the flames through the night, later assessed structural integrity, though officials have not yet confirmed whether the building is at risk of total collapse. The French Coastguard and national gendarmerie have opened a criminal investigation into the suspected arson, treating the act as a deliberate attack on public property and cultural heritage.

analysis.heading: Socio‑Political Context of the Protests
analysis.content: The arson coincides with a broader wave of demonstrations that have erupted across France since early October. Protesters, many affiliated with labour unions and opposition parties such as the National Rally (RN), have taken to the streets to denounce recent government reforms aimed at restructuring the public sector and tightening housing regulations. While the majority of demonstrations have remained peaceful, a small faction has resorted to violent tactics, including the targeting of symbolic government buildings. The Limoges attack appears to be an escalation that blends grievances over economic policy with a deeper sense of cultural alienation felt by some residents who view historic monuments as collateral damage in political disputes.

analysis.heading: Cultural Heritage Implications and Legal Ramifications
analysis.content: The destruction of a historic town hall raises urgent questions about the protection of France’s architectural heritage under the nation’s cultural‑property laws. The Ministry of Culture has pledged to assess the damage and explore emergency preservation measures, potentially invoking the "cordon sanitaire" protocol for endangered monuments. Legally, the act constitutes arson, a felony punishable by several years of imprisonment, and may be charged as an attack on a protected historical site, which carries enhanced penalties. Moreover, the incident could prompt a review of protest‑management strategies, balancing the right to demonstrate with the imperative to safeguard public heritage.

key_facts: The fire broke out on Saturday, 18 October 2026, destroying the 19th‑century Limoges town hall’s spire and causing extensive structural damage.
No casualties were reported, but the building’s overall stability remains uncertain pending a full engineering assessment.
French authorities have opened a criminal investigation for arson, treating the act as a deliberate assault on public property and cultural heritage.
The incident follows a nationwide series of protests against pension reforms and housing policy, with some demonstrators adopting more radical tactics.
Local residents expressed shock and condemnation, describing the attack as a selfish act that harms community identity.
implications: Potential escalation of protest violence could threaten other historic landmarks across France, prompting calls for enhanced security at cultural sites.
The case may set a legal precedent for harsher sentencing when heritage sites are targeted, influencing future judicial rulings on similar attacks.
The French government may reconsider its protest‑management approach, balancing civil liberties with the protection of national heritage.
items.outlook: The aftermath of the Limoges town‑hall fire will likely shape both the immediate security posture of French cultural sites and the broader political discourse surrounding protest tactics. If the investigation uncovers links to organised extremist elements, it could trigger a coordinated law‑enforcement response targeting networks that exploit social unrest to commit heritage crimes. Conversely, a perception that the attack was an isolated act of individual anger may reinforce calls for dialogue between the government and dissenting groups, aiming to address underlying economic grievances before they manifest in further acts of vandalism. In the longer term, the incident underscores the vulnerability of historic architecture in periods of social tension and may catalyse the implementation of more robust preventive measures, including real‑time monitoring and community‑based stewardship programs.

items.title: Major fire at Canada military base leaves four dead, dozens injured
items.tldr: A catastrophic fire at Canadian Forces Base Wainwright claimed four lives and injured dozens during high‑intensity live‑fire training, prompting national mourning and a wide‑ranging investigation. Prime Minister Mark Carney described the tragedy as one of the worst peacetime losses for the Canadian Armed Forces, while officials confirmed no terrorist link.
items.background: Canadian Forces Base Wainwright, located in Alberta, is one of the country’s primary live‑fire training hubs, hosting roughly 690 military personnel and 300 civilian staff on a typical day. The base conducts high‑intensity combat exercises, including grenade launches and artillery drills, to prepare troops for modern battlefield scenarios. Recent years have seen increased emphasis on safety protocols after several incidents at other NATO training facilities, yet the scale of operations means risks remain. The fire erupted on Saturday evening during such a training event, catching personnel off‑guard and overwhelming local emergency services.

analysis.heading: Operational Impact and Training Protocols
analysis.content: The blaze began while infantry units were executing a simulated enemy assault on a grenade range, with multiple ordnance types—grenade launchers, live grenades, small arms, and ammunition—present across the training area. Uncommonly strong winds accelerated the spread of a nearby grass fire, driving it toward the administrative sector of the range. The incident underscores potential gaps in real‑time fire detection during live‑munition exercises and raises questions about the safety margins set for wind conditions and the proximity of training zones to personnel areas.

analysis.heading: Emergency Response and Medical Coordination
analysis.content: Military and civilian emergency crews fought the flames throughout the night, operating in what Prime Minister Carney called "some of the worst conditions imaginable." The Royal Alexandra Hospital in Edmonton activated a Code Orange disaster protocol, deploying 30 units—including 22 ground ambulances, six fixed‑wing and two rotary‑wing aircraft—directly to Wainwright. STARS air ambulance services from Edmonton, Saskatoon, and Calgary also contributed, reflecting a coordinated regional response. The surge of patients overwhelmed local health facilities, prompting the provincial health agency to mobilise additional resources across Alberta.

analysis.heading: Geopolitical and Policy Implications
analysis.content: Prime Minister Mark Carney’s national address framed the loss as "one of the worst tragedies for the forces on Canadian soil in peacetime," reinforcing the human cost of military training. Canadian Armed Forces officials have already signalled that the investigation will focus on non‑terrorist origins, with Major General Wade Rutland stating the incident is not believed linked to oil and gas infrastructure or external interference. The tragedy is likely to spur a review of defence safety standards, potentially influencing NATO‑wide discussions on live‑fire training risk mitigation and prompting Canada to reassess its training doctrine and emergency preparedness frameworks.

key_facts: Fire broke out at approximately 16:00 local time (22:00 GMT) on Saturday at Canadian Forces Base Wainwright, Alberta.
Four Canadian military members—Sgt Morgan Wong, Pte Shaun Farrell, Pte Aidan Goulding, and Pte Hayden Lykkemark—have been confirmed dead.
Thirty‑nine injured personnel are being treated, with at least 19 in critical condition.
The cause remains under investigation; officials have ruled out terrorist activity and external interference.
Strong winds and a nearby grass fire contributed to the rapid spread toward the attack range.
The base typically hosts about 690 military personnel and 300 civilian workers daily.
implications: Potential revision of live‑fire training safety protocols and wind‑condition thresholds at Canadian bases.
Increased scrutiny of emergency response coordination between military and civilian agencies.
Impact on allied nations that share training facilities at Wainwright, possibly prompting a reassessment of joint exercise risk assessments.
Political pressure on the federal government to allocate additional funding for fire‑prevention infrastructure at military installations.
items.outlook: The investigation is expected to take several weeks, with preliminary findings likely to be released within ten days. In parallel, the Department of National Defence will convene a safety board to evaluate training procedures and recommend corrective actions. Should the board identify systemic weaknesses, legislative changes may follow, affecting both domestic defence policy and Canada’s contributions to NATO training initiatives. The broader international community will be watching for any shifts in how Western militaries balance realistic combat preparation with personnel safety.

items.fulltext:
Major fire at Canada military base leaves four dead, dozens injured
- Published
Four members of the Canadian military have died and dozens were injured in a major fire at a base in the province of Alberta.
Addressing the nation on Sunday from Ottawa, Prime Minister Mark Carney described it as "one of the worst tragedies for the forces on Canadian soil in peacetime".
The fire broke out at about 16:00 local time (22:00 GMT) on Saturday at Canadian Forces Base Wainwright, one of the country's busiest military training bases, and is now contained. Its cause is still unclear, but officials said it did not appear tied to "terrorist activity".
"The nation is in mourning for those brave members of our armed forces who we have lost," said Carney.
The BBC has confirmed that Sgt Morgan Wong, Pte Shaun Farrell, Pte Aidan Goulding and Pte Hayden Lykkemark have died.
Of the 39 injured people being cared for in hospital, at least 19 are in a critical condition, Alberta Premier Danielle Smith said at a press briefing on Sunday evening.
Fire and rescue teams are remaining at the scene to contain any potential flare-ups, Wainwright Mayor Bruce Pugh told the BBC.
Members of the infantry had been conducting "high-intensity combat training with live munitions" at a grenade range and attack range, where 10 soldiers practise attacking a simulated enemy, Maj-Gen Wade Rutland told reporters at the briefing.
"There was a multitude of ordnance moving through the Wainwright training area," he said, including a grenade launcher, grenades, small arms and ammunition.
A grass fire ignited about 1km (0.6 miles) away, with the cause currently under investigation, and moved toward the attack range.
"What I would say is there was multiple training activities happening throughout the training area at the time," he said. "Uncommonly strong winds caused the fire to spread rapidly and shift direction towards the range administrative area."
Cannon fire had been heard coming from the base on Saturday before it suddenly stopped, Mayor Pugh told the BBC, noting it's not uncommon to hear cannons being fired there.
News then came through that local emergency services had been deployed to an "all hands on deck" situation.
Carney said military and emergency crews fought the flames throughout the night in "some of the worst conditions imaginable".
The people who were hurt were on the attack range and included reservists and soldiers from the Princess Patricia's Canadian Light Infantry, officials said.
In a statement early on Sunday, the Canadian Armed Forces said that "while the incident remains under investigation, at this time, there are no indications that it was the result of any terrorist activity".
Rutland told the briefing: "We do not believe this [incident] to be a result of any oil and gas infrastructure nor any outside interference".
- What we know so far about deadly fire at Canadian military base 
  - Published1 hour ago
Wainwright, about 210km (130 miles) east of Edmonton, Alberta's capital, is one of the main bases used by the Canadian military for live-fire training exercises, and it houses troops from Canada and allied countries. About 690 military personnel and 300 civilian workers are on site on a typical day.
Warren Thirsk, an emergency department doctor at the Royal Alexandra Hospital, told broadcaster CBC that the number of patients involved in the incident had "completely overwhelmed" healthcare facilities in Wainwright.
The Royal Alexandra Hospital is in Edmonton, where patients are being transferred. The hospital at first declared a code orange - a disaster-response protocol for a high-casualty incident. That has since been stood down.
The provincial health agency said in a statement on Sunday that it deployed 30 units directly into Wainwright, including 22 ground ambulances, six fixed-wing and two rotary wing units.
"It is anticipated that care for patients impacted by this incident will be intensive and will add to existing high demand on acute care in Alberta," it said, adding that patients were being treated at facilities across the province.
STARS, the regional air ambulance service, said aircraft and crews from Edmonton, Saskatoon, and Calgary had been deployed.
Brandon Simmons, who lives in long-term care at the Wainwright Health Centre, told Reuters that when code orange was announced, nurses dropped everything and immediately started grabbing stretchers, gurneys and medical equipment before running to the front entrance.
Ambulances kept coming "throughout the night", he said.
"I heard people screaming inside of those vehicles that will never end up being out of my mind," he recalled, saying it was "like a scene from a war movie".
Additional reporting by Lisa Lambert

items.title: Polanski says he will not overturn Green Party's 'Zionism is racism' motion
items.tldr: Zack Polanski, leader of the UK Green Party, has refused to overturn a controversial motion declaring Zionism a form of racism, citing party rules that lock the policy in place until 2028. The motion, passed by a narrow member vote, has sparked internal division, external backlash from Jewish groups, and threatens the party's standing in upcoming elections.
items.background: The motion was approved at the Green Party’s conference earlier this month, defining Zionism as an ideology that supports “an ethnonationalist Jewish state in historic Palestine to the exclusion and/or domination of the non‑Jewish population.” It also calls for a single democratic state across historic Palestine, a full arms embargo on Israel, and support for Palestinian liberation. The vote—1,022 to 813—represented a tiny fraction of the party’s 230,000 members, highlighting the role of a highly motivated minority in shaping policy. Polanski, who previously said he would not have backed the motion without two amendments, now says he respects the democratic will of the membership, even though the decision has drawn criticism from MPs, Jewish campaigners, the government, and the European Green movement. The equality watchdog has written to the party seeking clarification, while Labour has threatened to end power‑sharing agreements with Greens on local councils unless the motion is disowned.

analysis.heading: Leadership Dilemma and Democratic Constraints
analysis.content: Polanski’s stance illustrates the tension between a leader’s personal convictions and the procedural rigidity of a participatory political party. Under the Green Party’s rule book, a motion passed at the annual conference becomes binding policy for two years, leaving the leadership with limited authority to reverse it. Polanski’s refusal to overturn the motion, despite his own reservations, underscores a broader principle: respect for member‑driven decision‑making, even when the outcome is politically toxic. This adherence to internal democracy, however, has exposed a structural vulnerability—policy can be captured by a relatively small, highly mobilised cohort, locking the party into positions that may alienate the broader electorate and its own elected representatives. The case raises questions about whether the Green Party’s governance model needs recalibration to balance grassroots empowerment with electoral viability.

analysis.heading: Impact on the Green Party’s Electoral Prospects
analysis.content: The fallout from the motion has already begun to affect the party’s electoral calculus. In the recent Holborn and St Pancras by‑election, Polanski finished second to Labour, a result that many analysts attribute to the backlash over the Zionism policy. Councillors across the country report heightened voter hostility, and Labour’s threat to sever local‑government pacts with the Greens adds a further layer of institutional pressure. Moreover, the motion has become a focal point for media narratives that portray the Greens as extremist on foreign policy, potentially eroding support among centrist voters who might otherwise be attracted to the party’s environmental agenda. The internal discord also hampers the party’s ability to present a unified front on climate and social justice issues, risking a feedback loop where policy controversy fuels electoral decline, which in turn weakens the party’s capacity to influence policy.

analysis.heading: Broader Geopolitical Repercussions
analysis.content: Beyond the UK’s domestic politics, the motion reverberates through the wider European and Middle‑Eastern diplomatic landscape. The European Green movement has expressed disappointment, warning that the language used could be interpreted as legitimising anti‑Semitic discourse, while the Board of Deputies of British Jews has accused the party of erasing Jewish identity and endorsing the elimination of Israel. In the context of ongoing Israel‑Palestine tensions, the motion’s endorsement of a single democratic state and an arms embargo places the Greens at odds with mainstream European Union positions, potentially complicating cross‑border cooperation on peace initiatives. Additionally, the controversy highlights the growing challenge for Western democratic parties in navigating the fine line between supporting Palestinian rights and avoiding language that can be construed as anti‑Jewish, a dilemma that will likely shape future debates on foreign policy and human‑rights legislation across the continent.

key_facts: The motion passed 1,022‑813 at the Green Party conference, representing less than 0.5 % of the party’s total membership.
Polanski says the policy is locked in until 2028 due to party rules and cannot be amended now.
The motion defines Zionism as an ideology supporting an ethnonationalist Jewish state to the exclusion of non‑Jewish populations.
The Green Party’s stance includes support for a single democratic state across historic Palestine, a full arms embargo on Israel, and Palestinian liberation.
The equality watchdog has written to the Greens seeking clarification on the motion’s implications.
Labour has threatened to end power‑sharing agreements with Greens on local councils unless the motion is disowned.
implications: Internal party cohesion is at risk, with senior figures like Adrian Ramsay calling for earlier policy review.
Electoral performance may suffer as voters react negatively to the controversial foreign‑policy position.
Cross‑party cooperation on local government could be disrupted by Labour’s threat to sever ties.
The motion may influence the European Green movement’s stance on Israel‑Palestine, potentially causing diplomatic friction.
The controversy could spur a broader debate within democratic parties about how to address Palestinian rights without alienating Jewish constituents.
items.outlook: Unless the Green Party can reconcile its internal democratic procedures with the electoral and diplomatic costs of the current policy, the controversy is likely to persist and further strain the party’s leadership. A potential pathway forward involves either a membership ballot to reaffirm or revise the motion, or a procedural amendment to allow leadership discretion in policy reversal. The party’s ability to navigate this challenge will shape not only its own trajectory but also the broader discourse on how progressive movements balance principle with political pragmatism in an increasingly polarised global environment.

items.fulltext:
Polanski says he will not overturn Green Party's 'Zionism is racism' motion
- Published
Zack Polanski has said he will not overturn a motion passed by Green Party members that declared Zionism a form of racism.
The Green leader told Sunday with Laura Kuenssberg that, while he would like to make amendments, it would be party policy until 2028.
The motion, passed at the party's conference earlier this month, described Zionism as an ideology supporting "an ethnonationalist Jewish state in historic Palestine to the exclusion and/or domination of the non-Jewish population".
It divided the party and sparked a major backlash from MPs, Jewish campaigners, the government and the European Green movement, with the equality watchdog writing to the party for more information on it.
The fallout from the motion overshadowed the final days of Polanski's campaign in the Holborn and St Pancras by-election, in which he came second to Labour, and threatened his leadership.
He came under criticism for not voting on the motion which was passed by 1,022 votes to 813 - a small fraction of the party's 230,000 members - in Brighton earlier this month.
The motion also asserted the party's backing for "a single democratic state throughout historic Palestine", a full arms embargo on Israel and a commitment to Palestinian liberation.
Asked if he would now step in as leader to overturn it, Polanski said: "I'm not going to try to overturn it.
"At the first available opportunity, I do want to amend it - I want to move away from one state, towards saying that Israelis and Palestinians should decide that future for themselves."
He said this would not be until 2028 as "you can't [amend it] within the rules, so when you vote on something in our party conference that's then policy for two years".
Kuenssberg asked if he would therefore change the rules as leader, but Polanski said: "I think if members have made a decision, then I respect the democratic will of our members."
Former Green Party co-leader and current MP Adrian Ramsay responded by calling for action to be taken sooner.
"I don't think it's tenable for us to continue the next two years with this policy that's been adopted given the huge political distraction that it's been for our councillors across the country," he told the BBC News Channel.
"One way forward could be to have a ballot of all party members to establish very clearly where does the party as a whole stand - my view is we would see a different answer."
Polanski had previously said he would not have voted for the motion without two amendments.
The first of these would have avoided "determining there was a single democratic state", and the other would have specified that the motion should not be used to discipline Jewish Green members who attend synagogues that consider themselves Zionist.
Both of these amendments were voted down by members at the party's conference.
Green MPs, including Ellie Chowns, have called for the party's member-led decision-making procedures to be reviewed given how few people took part in the vote.
'All over the place'
Asked if he thought Zionism was racist, Polanski said he did not think this was controversial, adding: "I think what's controversial is that 75,000 Palestinians have been murdered in the last few years."
Kuenssberg asked Polanski if he accepted that for many Jewish people, Zionism was the right to have a safe place to live, or homeland.
"I think that's what people think it means, but actually in practical application - which is what we're talking about here - that homeland has come to the cost of the Palestinian people," Polanski, who is Jewish, said.
"I want equal rights for Israelis and Palestinians - the practical application of Zionism has not resulted in that."
When questioned if he thought Israel had a right to exist, he said he did not think "any state has a right to exist under international law".
And asked if he would apologise for his handling of the row, as the Jewish Greens chair Vivien Lichtenstein has asked him to do, Polanski said: "I'm not sorry at all."
In response, Phil Rosenberg, president of the Board of Deputies of British Jews, accused Polanski of being "all over the place" on the issue.
"Let us remember that, as of now, the Green Party's platform erases Jewish identity and experience, calls for Israel's elimination, and tells the vast majority of Jews, who overwhelmingly believe in the right of Israel to exist, that they are not welcome in the party," Rosenberg added.
Polanski has said no Jewish Green members will be excluded based on their faith or background - and that being Jewish and supporting Israel are "two separate things".
His latest comments come after a fortnight of criticism from across the political spectrum over the motion.
Labour has said it will end power-sharing agreements with the Greens on local councils, unless its councillors disown the motion while Prime Minister Andy Burnham called it "antisemitic". Polanski said it was up to Green councillors to do what they saw fit.

items.title: Ending corridor care in hospitals for children a priority, says health secretary
items.tldr: Health Secretary Yvette Cooper has declared an urgent push to end children’s hospital corridor care, backed by a £140 m investment in urgent care. The announcement follows the tragic death of two‑year‑old Finlay Roberts in a UK A&E corridor and aims to improve standards and data collection for paediatric emergency treatment.
items.background: The NHS has long struggled with overcrowding, especially in emergency departments, leading to “corridor care” where patients receive treatment in hallways or waiting rooms. Recent summer heatwaves caused record A&E admissions, exacerbating existing capacity issues. The government’s previous manifesto pledge to end corridor care for all patients by the end of the parliament has not been met, prompting a renewed focus on the most vulnerable group—children. The case of Finlay Roberts, who died in 2024 after hours in a north‑London corridor, has become a rallying point for reform.

analysis.heading: Policy Prioritisation and Funding
analysis.content: Cooper’s announcement signals a shift from a broad, delayed target to a specific, urgent priority for children. The £140 m allocation is intended to fund 14 schemes across England, ranging from new urgent‑care centres to ambulance fleet upgrades and emergency‑department enhancements. This targeted funding reflects an acknowledgment that systemic change requires both capital investment and measurable benchmarks, such as age‑disaggregated corridor‑care data, to track progress.

analysis.heading: Operational Challenges and Workforce Strain
analysis.content: Despite the financial injection, the NHS faces a “twin crisis” of seasonal demand and chronic staffing shortages. The Royal College of Nursing warns that the extra money is a “sticking plaster” on a system already at breaking point. Nursing vacancies, burnout, and the impending winter surge of flu and norovirus threaten to overwhelm the very services the funding aims to bolster, raising questions about the sustainability of short‑term fixes.

analysis.heading: Political and Public Reaction
analysis.content: The government’s move has been welcomed by health advocacy groups, who have long called for an end to corridor care, but critics, including Shadow Health Secretary Damian Hinds, demand transparency on funding sources. The broader 2029 manifesto commitment—92 % of patients starting treatment within 18 weeks—remains unmet after more than a decade, prompting skepticism about whether the new paediatric focus will be enough to restore public confidence in NHS timeliness and safety.

key_facts: Health Secretary Yvette Cooper has ordered the NHS to produce urgent plans to end corridor care for children.
A new £140 m investment will fund 14 urgent‑care projects, including new centres and ambulance upgrades.
For the first time, corridor‑care data will be collected by age group in English A&E departments.
Two‑year‑old Finlay Roberts died in 2024 after spending hours in a north‑London hospital corridor.
NHS England recorded 7.37 million treatments awaiting completion at the end of August 2026, a historic summer peak.
The government’s 2029 manifesto target of 92 % of patients starting treatment within 18 weeks remains unmet.
implications: Improved data collection will enable targeted interventions and accountability for paediatric emergency care.
Additional funding may alleviate immediate capacity pressures but does not address underlying staffing deficits.
The focus on children could set a precedent for prioritising vulnerable patient groups in broader NHS reform.
Political scrutiny over funding sources may influence future health‑policy budgeting and transparency requirements.
items.outlook: If the £140 m funding is effectively deployed, the short‑term outlook for paediatric emergency care could see reduced corridor usage and faster discharge times. However, without a concurrent strategy to recruit and retain nursing staff, the gains may be temporary. The government will need to balance immediate investment with long‑term systemic reforms to meet the 2029 manifesto target and restore public trust in the NHS’s ability to provide dignified, timely care for all patients, especially children.

items.fulltext:
Ending corridor care in hospitals for children a priority, says health secretary
- Published
The health secretary has asked the NHS to draw up urgent plans to speed up ending hospital "corridor care" for children.
Yvette Cooper told the BBC there would be new standards for caring for children in A&E in England, with figures collected on corridor care by age for the first time.
She was speaking on Sunday with Laura Kuenssberg where the programme highlighted the case of two-year-old Finlay Roberts who died in 2024 after spending hours in a hospital corridor before being discharged.
The health secretary has announced Â£140m to improve urgent care in England ahead of what she said would be a "more difficult" winter than usual.
The government has already pledged to end corridor care for all patients by the end of this parliament, and now Cooper has said eradicating it for children would be prioritised.
Corridor care refers to patients receiving treatment or waiting in corridors, waiting rooms or other hospital areas due to a lack of appropriate space.
The health secretary was also asked if the government would meet a key manifesto pledge that 92% of patients would start treatment within 18 weeks of booking a hospital appointment by 2029.
"That remains our manifesto commitment and of course we're going to keep working towards it," Cooper said.
Pushed further on whether the target was achievable, she replied: "The whole point about having the targets is about having something stretching that we work towards."
The 18-week target has consistently not been met for more than a decade.
Cooper said that the NHS was dealing with a number of challenges after record A&E admissions following heatwaves over the summer.
According to the latest figures for England, an estimated 7.37 million treatments were waiting to be carried out at the end of August, relating to 6.24 million patients.
On the programme the story of Finlay Roberts, was highlighted. He died after being discharged from hospital in 2024 following hours spent in an A&E corridor in north London.
Finlay's father David told the BBC the situation was a "terrible mess", with the family moved into a room with a bed before being moved back into the corridor.
"He just clung to me, as we now know, slowly dying," he said.
Liz Roberts, Finlay's mother, said corridor care "robs people of their dignity when they are at their most vulnerable". She recalled being told to administer a suppository to her son in the corridor.
Cooper apologised to Finlay's parents on behalf of the NHS, saying: "No child should be treated in a corridor. No patient should be treated in a corridor."
The Whittington Health NHS Trust where this happened extended their condolences to the family.
They said they continued to experience periods of exceptional demand across emergency care and at times some patients may receive care in temporary clinical areas, including corridors.
"Our staff work tirelessly to provide safe and compassionate care in extremely challenging conditions," they said.
On Friday health groups - including Age UK, Marie Curie and the Royal College of Nursing (RCN), also expressed their concern over corridor care, writing a letter to the health secretary urging her to take action.
It said the practice was fundamentally incompatible with NHS care standards and it would require "whole-system action" to eradicate it.
This weekend Cooper announced Â£140m funding to boost urgent care capacity as part of an effort to deal with the impact of seasonal illnesses, including flu and norovirus.
The money will go towards 14 schemes across England, including new urgent care centres, ambulance fleets and upgrades to emergency departments.
Shadow health secretary Damian Hinds said the government needed to act, but asked it to explain where the money was coming from.
It comes after almost 7.3 million people attended A&E between June and August in England, according to NHS data, the highest ever figure for a summer period.
Health thinktank the King's Fund warned that the service was facing a "twin crisis" going into the winter, with little time between peak periods for staff and the system to recover.
NHS leaders are urging eligible people to get flu vaccinations, with medical director Prof Frankie Swords saying earlier this month there were "ominous" signs of winter pressure already affecting hospitals.
Swords said there were more patients coming to A&E with flu and other respiratory viruses than usual for this time of year.
RCN England's executive director Patricia Marquis said the extra money was welcome but would ultimately provide "just another sticking plaster on a system that is at breaking point".
"The nursing workforce needed to deliver these services goes into winter already running on empty and short of staff," she said.
Correction 18 October 2026: This article and this note have been updated after earlier versions incorrectly stated the location of Finlay Roberts' death.
